title: us is helping fuel chinese factories its competing with 2026 07 29
author: Gavin Maguire
text:
LITTLETON, Colorado, July 29 (Reuters) - A curious pattern is emerging in U.S.-China trade.
Washington has spent years trying to rebuild domestic manufacturing, reduce dependence on Chinese supply chains and shift strategic production back to American soil.
Yet commodity flows suggest the United States is simultaneously becoming an increasingly important supplier of the raw materials that keep China's industrial ​machine running.
The relationship is evolving, not disappearing.
While imports of finished Chinese goods have become politically contentious, exports of U.S. energy, petrochemical feedstocks and agricultural commodities continue to provide critical inputs ‌for Chinese industry.
The result is a deeply complementary relationship that may be undermining the United States' broader ambitions to reclaim manufacturing leadership.
The clearest example is ethane.
U.S. ethane exports to China reached a record of close to 1 million metric tons in March 2026 and totaled 5 million tons during the first half of the year, data from commodities intelligence firm Kpler shows.
All told, U.S. ethane shipments to China are up roughly 88% from the same period of 2025.
Propane shipments remained substantial ​at 5.77 million tons over the same period, while butane shipments more than doubled year-on-year.
Those are not consumer products. They are industrial building blocks.
Ethane is cracked into ethylene, the foundation of plastics, ​packaging, synthetic fibers, industrial chemicals and countless manufactured products. Propane and butane play similar roles in China's expanding petrochemical sector.
U.S. shale fields are increasingly supplying the molecules ⁠that feed Chinese factories.
In effect, the two economies may be settling into a new division of labor.
The United States extracts hydrocarbons, grows crops and exports raw materials. China converts those inputs into chemicals, plastics, components ​and finished goods.
That arrangement makes economic sense. American shale producers possess a cost advantage in natural gas liquids. Chinese firms possess vast manufacturing ecosystems, dense supplier networks and enormous processing capacity. Each side specializes where it ​is strongest.
The problem for Washington is that this logic points in the opposite direction of industrial policy.
The objective of recent U.S. policy has not simply been to maximize export earnings. It has been to rebuild domestic industrial capabilities.
Success is supposed to be measured not only by how much the U.S. produces, but by how much value is added within its borders.
Selling molecules rather than manufactured products does not necessarily achieve that goal.
From an industrial policy perspective, the biggest prize is not ​extracting ethane. It is converting it into higher-value products. Profits, jobs, technological know-how and export opportunities often lie further downstream in the value chain.
China appears to understand this.
The country's imports from the U.S. increasingly resemble ​the raw ingredients of manufacturing rather than manufacturing itself.
Alongside rising ethane shipments, Chinese purchases of U.S. sorghum surged more than 3 million tons year-on-year during January to June, while soybean imports climbed by nearly 5 million tons. Imports of ‌petroleum coke ⁠and other industrial inputs also rose.
Collectively, these flows look less like a decoupling story than a supply-chain story.
The United States is exporting feedstocks. China is importing those inputs and using them to support industrial activity.
That raises an uncomfortable question: can the U.S. realistically restore manufacturing leadership while simultaneously becoming a key supplier of the raw materials needed by Chinese manufacturers?
History suggests this can be difficult.
Commodity exporters often find themselves capturing less value than countries specializing in processing and manufacturing.
The industrialized economies that dominate global value chains tend to be those that transform raw materials into complex products rather than those that simply produce the underlying inputs.
The U.S. is ​obviously far more diversified than a typical commodity exporter. ​Yet the direction of travel in trade with ⁠China increasingly resembles a classic upstream-downstream relationship.
Indeed, the irony is that growing geopolitical tensions may reinforce rather than weaken the arrangement.
Disruptions to Middle Eastern energy supplies, including those associated with conflict involving Iran, increase the attractiveness of secure U.S.-sourced feedstocks.
Chinese buyers seeking supply reliability may therefore find themselves turning even more frequently toward American ​ethane, propane and other industrial ingredients.
If so, strategic rivalry could actually deepen commercial interdependence in certain sectors rather than eliminate it.
For U.S. policymakers, that creates ​a dilemma.
Encouraging exports benefits producers, ⁠supports jobs and improves the trade balance. Restricting exports would be economically painful and politically unpopular.
Yet every cargo of ethane delivered to a Chinese cracker potentially strengthens the competitiveness of the very industrial ecosystem Washington is attempting to challenge.
The emerging reality is that America and China are not decoupling so much as specializing.
America increasingly supplies the molecules. China increasingly supplies the manufacturing.
And as long as that complementary relationship persists, Washington may discover that rebuilding a globally ⁠dominant manufacturing base ​is harder than tariff schedules and industrial subsidies alone can solve.
The United States can compete with China's factories. But it may ​first have to stop feeding them.
The opinions expressed here are those of the author, a columnist for Reuters.
